text: This lab walks through building a tiny, fully worked quantum kernel matrix for a 3-point toy dataset by hand, then uses it to make a classification decision the way a support vector machine would.

Three one-feature data points, angle-encoded. Point A at x equals 0.4, labeled zero. Point B at x equals 0.5, labeled zero, close to A. And point C at x equal to about 4.3416, labeled one, deliberately placed roughly opposite A on the encoding circle to guarantee a clearly separable case.

Using the cosine-squared kernel formula, the full kernel matrix comes out to: k of A and B about 0.9975, nearly maximally similar, since A and B's x-values are close. k of A and C about 0.1516, and k of B and C about 0.1176 — both quite dissimilar. Every point with itself gives exactly 1.0, as always.

Now classify a new point D at x equals 0.45. Its kernel value against A is about 0.9994, against B also about 0.9994, since D sits exactly between them, and against C only about 0.1342. D is far more similar to A and B, labeled zero, than to C, labeled one, so the kernel-weighted call predicts label zero for D — matching intuition, since D's raw value of 0.45 sits right between A's 0.4 and B's 0.5.

Chapter 4 opens next with quantum neural network architectures, a name borrowed from classical deep learning — useful, but imperfect, and this lesson is precise about exactly where that analogy breaks down.
